prompt: How many pairs of people may need to talk in a group of 12?
What does Brooks's law say?

choices.text: Adding people to a late project makes it later
choices.why: Right. New people need training and add paths to coordinate.

choices.text: Work expands to fill the time available
choices.why: That is Parkinson's law.

choices.text: Teams of more than ten are slower
choices.why: Brooks's law is about adding people late, not a size limit.

choices.text: Systems mirror the communication structure of whoever builds them
choices.why: That is Conway's law, from 1968.

prompt: Three teams are split by layer: screens, API, database. By Conway's law, what follows for features?

choices.text: Features stay inside one team
choices.why: That happens when teams are split by product area.

choices.text: The teams merge into one
choices.why: Nothing forces a merge; the dependencies are what result.

choices.text: Each feature crosses all three teams
choices.why: Right. The system has strong layers, and every feature carries three-way dependencies.

choices.text: Conway's law says nothing about features, only about meetings
choices.why: It is about system structure, which decides where features cut.

prompt: What does the lesson name as the cost scaling frameworks are mostly about?
hint: A feature waits for the slowest backlog.

choices.text: The salaries of a larger organisation
choices.why: Real, but not what the frameworks coordinate.

choices.text: Office space for planning events that need everybody in one room
choices.why: A logistics cost, not the core problem.

choices.text: Dependencies between teams
choices.why: Right. A feature that needs three teams is finished when the slowest gets to it.

choices.text: Licences for the tools
choices.why: Tools are not what makes scale hard.

prompt: How many people does a SAFe Agile Release Train typically have?

choices.text: Exactly 100, by the framework's rules
choices.why: The framework gives a range, not a fixed number.
Right. Enough for several teams, few enough to plan in one room.

choices.text: 5 to 11, like one Scrum Team
choices.why: That is one team, not a train.

choices.text: Up to 1,000
choices.why: Far beyond what one train can plan together.

prompt: Match each SAFe train role to its nearest Scrum equivalent or its job.
hint: One level up from a team.

pairs.right: A Scrum Master for the train
A Product Owner for the train

prompt: What is the architectural runway, in SAFe?

choices.text: The deployment pipeline only
choices.why: Infrastructure is part of it, but runway is broader.

choices.text: The base later features build on
choices.why: Right. Existing code and infrastructure that let upcoming features be built without delay; it must be extended deliberately or the train slows down.

choices.text: The architect's slides for the business owners
choices.why: Slides do not let features be built faster.

choices.text: The two days of PI Planning
choices.why: That is an event, not a body of code.

prompt: Which SAFe configuration addresses how much money each value stream receives?

choices.text: Large Solution
choices.why: It coordinates several trains on one system, not funding.

choices.text: Portfolio
choices.why: Right. It sits above the trains and decides funding.

choices.text: Essential
choices.why: The core: one or more trains, no funding layer.

choices.text: Team
choices.why: Not one of the four configurations.

prompt: In the common ten-week Planning Interval, how many iterations are there, counting the IP iteration?
Why does the lesson warn against filling the IP iteration with features?

choices.text: Features built in it cannot be released
choices.why: Nothing stops release; the problem is the lost slack.

choices.text: SAFe forbids any work in it on pain of losing certification
choices.why: The warning is about the plan's margin, not a penalty.

choices.text: It is the train's slack
choices.why: Right. Without it, the plan has no margin for what nobody foresaw.

choices.text: It is only one day long
choices.why: It is a full iteration, usually two weeks.

prompt: What does a release train leave PI Planning with? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Each developer's individual targets
choices.why: Objectives are per team, not per person.

choices.text: A planning board showing features and dependencies
choices.why: Yes: the ART planning board.

choices.text: PI objectives per team, with business value
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A confidence vote
choices.why: Yes: fingers from one to five.

choices.text: A signed fixed-price contract
choices.why: Nothing in PI Planning is a contract.

prompt: What does the lesson say is the main value of PI Planning?

choices.text: The certification it gives participants
choices.why: PI Planning gives nobody a certificate.

choices.text: Dependencies negotiated in hours, face to face
choices.why: Right. The room is the value; a plan treated as a contract is the risk.

choices.text: Removing the need for team retrospectives
choices.why: Teams keep their own events.

choices.text: A fixed ten-week plan nobody may change
choices.why: That is the risk the lesson names, not the value.

prompt: Risks raised in PI Planning are sorted as resolved, owned, accepted or mitigated, a scheme known by the letters ___.
How many Product Owners does LeSS have for a product built by six teams?

choices.text: None; the teams order the backlog
choices.why: One person owns the product.

choices.text: Six, one per team
choices.why: That is the arrangement LeSS rejects.

choices.text: Two, a chief and a deputy
choices.why: LeSS names no deputy.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right. One Product Owner, one backlog, one Definition of Done, one Sprint.

prompt: What happens in LeSS's Sprint Planning One?
hint: All teams, with the Product Owner.

choices.text: The managers set each team's targets for the Sprint
choices.why: Managers do not plan the Sprint.

choices.text: The architect approves the design of every item
choices.why: LeSS has no architect role.

choices.text: Which items each team takes
choices.why: Right. Planning Two is where each team plans how.

choices.text: Each team plans its tasks on its own
choices.why: That is Sprint Planning Two.

prompt: Who attends LeSS's Overall Retrospective, and what does it look at?
hint: The system the teams work in.

choices.text: Stakeholders, reviewing the increment
choices.why: That is the Sprint Review.

choices.text: Only the managers, reviewing team performance
choices.why: It is not a performance review.

choices.text: Team delegates and managers; the organisation
choices.why: Right. Team representatives, Scrum Masters, the Product Owner and managers look at the system the teams work in; each team still has its own retrospective.

choices.text: Every member of every team, replacing team retrospectives
choices.why: Team retrospectives remain.

prompt: An organisation wants LeSS but refuses to change any team's structure. What does the lesson predict?

choices.text: It will find LeSS impossible
choices.why: Right. LeSS removes coordination by changing structure; without that change it has nothing to work with.

choices.text: It should switch to LeSS Huge
choices.why: LeSS Huge makes the same demands at larger scale.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since LeSS adds no roles
choices.why: Adding no roles is why structure has to change instead.

choices.text: It will adopt LeSS faster than SAFe
choices.why: The refusal blocks the very thing LeSS depends on.

prompt: Why does a feature like 'receptionists can move an appointment' get slow with component teams?

choices.text: It needs three teams' backlogs
choices.why: Right. It is finished when the last of the three reaches it.

choices.text: The database cannot change while the screens are being built
choices.why: Layers can change in parallel; the queues are the problem.

choices.text: Specialists write slower code
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.

choices.text: Component teams have fewer people
choices.why: Headcount is not the issue; hand-overs are.

prompt: Which costs of feature teams does the lesson ask an architect to name? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Features need three backlogs to finish
choices.why: That is the cost of component teams.

choices.text: Deep specialisms spread thin
choices.why: Yes: specialists work across teams.

choices.text: Shared code that nobody owns the design of
choices.why: Yes: answered by component communities and review.

choices.text: Some components are better kept with one team
choices.why: Yes: a platform or a regulated part.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the choice between feature and component teams an architectural decision?

choices.text: SAFe requires the System Architect to sign it off
choices.why: SAFe requires no such sign-off.

choices.text: Architects are paid to decide the organisation chart
choices.why: The point is the effect on the system, not who draws the chart.

choices.text: Team boundaries shape the system's boundaries
choices.why: Right. Teams split by layer produce a system of strong layers.

choices.text: Feature teams need a different programming language
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Where did the 'Spotify model' come from, according to the lesson?

choices.text: The Scrum Guide's chapter on scaling
choices.why: The Scrum Guide has no such chapter.

choices.text: SAFe's Large Solution configuration
choices.why: Unrelated to SAFe.

choices.text: A 2012 paper on Spotify's teams
choices.why: Right. It was never a framework, and the company changed it afterwards.

choices.text: A certification body that licenses it
choices.why: Nobody certifies it.

prompt: Before adopting a scaling framework, which question does the lesson put first?

choices.text: How many tools will the trains need?
choices.why: Tools come last.

choices.text: Could the work be split so teams depend on each other less?
choices.why: Right. Removing coordination beats managing it.

choices.text: Which framework has the most certified people?
choices.why: Popularity does not reduce dependencies.

choices.text: Who will be the Release Train Engineer?
choices.why: That assumes SAFe before asking whether coordination is needed.

prompt: Match each scaling approach to its description.

pairs.right: Scrum for three to nine teams, with an integration team
One backlog and one Product Owner for up to eight teams
A toolkit for choosing a way of working

prompt: Two teams spend every PI Planning negotiating the same interface between their services. Which response does the lesson favour?

choices.text: Make PI Planning three days long
choices.why: More time to negotiate the same dependency is not a fix.

choices.text: Add a third team to coordinate the two
choices.why: That adds coordination instead of removing the need.

choices.text: Change the interface or the boundary so they stop depending on it
choices.why: Right. A week's change can remove a dependency that costs every quarter.

choices.text: Ask each team to plan without the other
choices.why: Ignoring the dependency does not remove it.
